Emma Tucker
 
North Korea Keeps Building Nukes—and Ghosting Trump
 
Plus, a new figure emerges in the Nvidia chip-smuggling saga, and the holiday gift guide for the techie (and nontechie) in your life
 
 
LINH PHAM/GETTY IMAGES
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

With so much attention focused on conflicts elsewhere, North Korea’s growing nuclear threat has largely slipped out of the spotlight.

 

On Friday, we reported that new satellite images show an expansion of a North Korean uranium-enrichment plant. And that’s just part of a much bigger story. Since Kim Jong Un last met President Trump in 2019, his nuclear arsenal has grown to an estimated 60 warheads. Meanwhile, Trump’s hopes of reconnecting have gone unrealized. One letter from the White House was even tossed aside, unopened, by a North Korean diplomat.

 

Today, our reporters explain how Kim has strengthened his position through closer ties with Russia, massive cryptocurrency thefts and a growing nuclear stockpile—all while resisting Trump’s overtures.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• The United Arab Emirates is shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz with U.S. military protection, braving Iranian attacks to keep crude flowing and help break Tehran’s grip on the waterway.

 

• Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has outlasted administration rivals despite scrutiny over the Nvidia scandal and his family’s Wall Street firm, aided by his longtime friendship with Trump.

 

• Ukraine’s defense industry—reborn since Russia invaded the country—has likely reached a ceiling, according to industry officials and defense analysts.

 

• Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is struggling to stabilize an agency in crisis, as a series of missteps renews calls within the Trump administration to replace him.

 

• After a week of tech disruptions, here’s how to prepare for the next bank outage. Plus, tips to protect yourself from scammers exploiting the chaos.

 
 
 

3. FROM THE MARKETS

 

• The AI selloff ravaging the stock market in recent weeks is remarkably like the bursting of the dot-com bubble, writes James Mackintosh.

 

• Robert Pattinson’s bare wrist in the James Bond announcement has watch collectors wondering whether 007 will ditch Omega after three decades for Jaeger-LeCoultre, writes Carol Ryan.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

A new figure emerges in the Nvidia chip-smuggling saga.

 

Alice Huang, the romantic partner of ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, was the public face of Megaspeed, a Singapore company suspected of funneling advanced computing power to China. But behind the scenes was Li Ming, a 52-year-old Chinese national now facing fraud charges in Singapore. Li was deeply involved in Megaspeed’s activities and major decisions, while also playing a role in other companies trading Nvidia chips. Stu Woo uncovers the previously unreported connections behind a scandal that brought down one of Silicon Valley’s biggest names.

 

5.

 

Baby boomers are rewriting the rules of growing old.

 

This year, the oldest boomers are turning 80, and many are approaching their later years with bigger expectations. Rather than slowing down, they’re traveling the world, staying active and even moving into larger homes. Their collective wealth, now exceeding $97 trillion, is also reshaping the U.S. economy. But not everyone can afford this new vision of aging. Rachel Louise Ensign examines how boomers are changing what it means to grow old.

 
 
 

The economics of growing old.
From rising elder-care costs to the challenges of caring for aging parents, our new series explores how America’s aging population is reshaping household finances and everyday life. Sign up for Personal Finance alerts for updates on this series.

 
 
 

6. SEE THE STORY

 

Inside the kitchen of a cookbook star.

 
 
ELIZABETH ARVELOS COETZEE/WSJ
 

Award-winning cookbook author Andy Baraghani has opened his first restaurant, Ditto, in New York City. Now he’s giving us a look inside his own stainless-steel kitchen, which he preserved while renovating the rest of his home. Explore his carefully stocked pantry, favorite cooking tools and the making of his chile and citrusy yogurt-brined roast chicken. Plus, get the recipe to try at home.

 
 
 

7. HAPPENING THIS WEEK

 

• Monday: S&P Global releases preliminary November readings of U.S. manufacturing and services activity. Hewlett Packard Enterprise, Agilent Technologies, Zoom report earnings.

 

• Tuesday: The Conference Board releases its November consumer-confidence index. Dell Technologies, Analog Devices, Medtronic, Autodesk, Workday report earnings.

 

• Wednesday: The Commerce Department releases the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge, the October personal-consumption expenditures price index, along with an updated estimate of third-quarter GDP. The Fed releases its Beige Book report on economic conditions. Deere reports earnings.

 

• Thursday: Americans celebrate Thanksgiving. U.S. stock and bond markets are closed.

 

• Friday: Black Friday kicks off the holiday shopping season. U.S. stock markets close early at 1 p.m. ET.

 
 
 

8. THE NUMBER

 
60%
 

The interest rate a Mexican drug gang charged borrowers over 14 weeks after taking over a microlending operation in the Mexican city of Zacapu, tripling the previous rate. Criminal groups are increasingly forcing small lenders out of business and taking control of loans that many low-income entrepreneurs depend on. Once gangs take over, access to capital becomes far more expensive—and dangerous.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

The holiday gift guide for the techie (and nontechie) in your life.

 

From a smart ring that records your fleeting thoughts to a tiny robot that presses buttons for you, our Personal Tech columnist Nicole Nguyen has rounded up her 15 favorite gadgets of 2026. The best part? You don’t need to spend a fortune to find something worth giving.
